summary: Summarizes the requirements of research and academic network users for network access to multimedia information. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A list of what scientists and students need so they can get pictures, sound and video over the network.

subtitle: Research and academic users' requirements for accessing multimedia over the network.

tldr.problem: Research and academic users need to access multimedia information like images, video and audio over networks, but existing systems like Gopher and Web have gaps in multimedia support.
tldr.mechanism: This technical report surveys user requirements from multiple application domains, evaluates existing systems and standards, and identifies the differences between current capabilities and actual needs.
tldr.outcome: The report recommends that RARE focus efforts on enhancing the World-Wide Web with better multimedia support, conversion tools, and quality of service improvements rather than building new systems.

today: RFC 1614 is an Informational RFC from May 1994. It is a historical technical report documenting the multimedia capabilities gap between user requirements and deployed systems in 1994. The report's recommendations on enhancing the World-Wide Web proved prescient: the Web ultimately became the dominant platform for multimedia information access. However, the specific systems, standards, and products discussed (Gopher, WAIS, Hyper-G, SGML authoring tools) were largely displaced by Web-based technologies and have limited relevance today.

sections.title: The Challenge of Networked Multimedia
sections.content:
This RFC is a technical report on a practical problem: research and academic communities want to access multimedia information—stored audio, video clips, images, and entire multimedia applications—across networks remotely. At the time of writing in 1994, few commercial products addressed this, and the applicability of existing standards was unclear.

The report investigates projects planned or underway in the community and examines existing information systems such as Gopher, WAIS (Wide Area Information Server), and the emerging World-Wide Web to assess their multimedia support. It also studies hypermedia systems emerging from research and reviews relevant standards, identifying gaps between what is available and what users actually need.
sections.plainLanguage: Scientists need to see pictures and videos over the Internet, but the tools available in 1994 were not very good at it. This report asks, 'What do people actually need? What exists today? What's missing?'

sections.title: What Users Actually Need
sections.content:
The report identifies requirements from four classes of applications: multimedia database applications (large collections of images and data with search capabilities), academic publishing (multiple media types with hyperlinking and various access methods), computer-aided learning (sophisticated presentation and synchronization), and general multimedia information services (on-line documentation and campus-wide systems).

Cross-cutting requirements include support for multiple platforms (Macintosh, UNIX, PC/MS Windows), a wide range of media types beyond text, hyperlinks between documents, sophisticated synchronization and presentation, database search techniques, user authentication and charging, response times under 20 seconds, and powerful authoring tools. User annotation of documents and the ability to execute scripts are also valued.
sections.plainLanguage: Different users need different things. Teachers need videos with timing. Database people need to search images. Everybody needs it to work on their computer and be fast.

sections.title: Existing Systems and Their Limits
sections.content:
Three main systems dominated the landscape in 1994: Gopher presents a hierarchical arrangement of documents and search nodes, with over 1000 servers deployed but lacks hyperlinks. WAIS (Wide Area Information Server) excels at full-text search of remote databases but handles non-text data poorly, indexing only by filename. The World-Wide Web offers true hypermedia with clickable links and distributed architecture, though it was still smaller than Gopher at the time.

All three systems fall short in several ways: there is little support for sophisticated presentation and synchronization; database queries remain limited to keyword search; response times vary widely with network distance and there is no support for time-sensitive (isochronous) data; authentication and charging facilities are minimal; and scripting is unsupported due to security concerns.
sections.plainLanguage: Gopher is like a library catalog—organized in folders but no cross-references. WAIS is like a search engine but can't handle pictures well. The Web is newer and has links between pages, but none of them handle multimedia really well.

sections.title: Advanced Research Systems
sections.content:
Several ambitious research projects point toward better solutions. Hyper-G at the University of Graz combines hypermedia, information retrieval, documentation, communication, and teaching with automatic hyperlink generation. Microcosm from Southampton is a PC-based framework layered on top of existing applications, allowing relationships between documents to be maintained separately from the data itself. AthenaMuse 2, developed at MIT, is a distributed authoring and presentation system with strong support for multimedia synchronization and networked delivery, planned as a commercial product.

The Xanadu project, while conceptually ambitious in designing open hypermedia, had not delivered a working system despite years of effort. Various European Commission research programmes (Esprit and RACE) also provided relevant contributions, though often directed toward commercial markets rather than academic applications.
sections.plainLanguage: Some universities are building experimental systems that might be better. Hyper-G has smart links. Microcosm works on top of what people already use. AthenaMuse 2 is being built with videos in mind from the start.

sections.title: Standards for Multimedia Hypermedia
sections.content:
Multiple standards address different aspects of multimedia information. SGML (Standard Generalized Markup Language) provides a flexible way to mark up the logical structure of documents and has become important in hypermedia systems. HyTime, standardized by ISO and built on SGML, offers powerful infrastructure for representing integrated hypermedia documents but is not optimized for runtime efficiency.

MHEG (Multimedia and Hypermedia information coding Experts Group) is an emerging draft ISO standard using object-oriented approaches, optimized for runtime efficiency. ODA (Open Document Architecture) was being enhanced for multimedia but interest was declining. Adobe's Acrobat PDF format provides a portable way to represent printable multimedia documents. MIME standards define media types and encoding methods for multimedia email with broader applicability. The report notes that full standardization remains incomplete and standards bodies and trade associations (IMA, MMCF) are actively working in this space.
sections.plainLanguage: SGML is a way to write down what a document means. HyTime is a standard for linking. MHEG is for multimedia apps. Acrobat is a format for documents. Standards are still being figured out.

sections.title: Recommendations for the Path Forward
sections.content:
The report identifies three common design themes across all systems and standards: content is distinct from hyperstructure, media type is distinct from media encoding, and data is distinct from protocol. It concludes that distributed hypermedia systems are moving from research into experimental deployment, but existing global systems still rely mainly on external viewers for non-textual data.

The most significant gaps between current capabilities and user requirements are in presentation and quality of service (responsiveness). The report recommends that RARE (a European research networking organization) focus its efforts on enhancing the World-Wide Web rather than building new systems. The reasons include the Web's flexible architecture, existing hyperlinks, ongoing multimedia enhancement efforts, its role as an integrating solution for both WAIS and Gopher, and its rapid growth rate despite Gopher's larger deployment at the time.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of building everything from scratch, focus on making the Web better. It already has links, it's growing fast, and lots of people are working to improve it.
